utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I assume that you are hearing me in a language that you can understand. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good morning to you. Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova and case manager Denise Gustin for the Prosecution. Your Honour, before we go on with the witness, may I return to something that I raised last night when we have done the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Sorry, I should explain, in the United Kingdom n England and Wales, you get strongly ticked off, corrected, if you say good morning to the Judge or the jury, and that's why -- I hope Your Honours don't think I'm being rude. It's not normal for me to say good morning to the Judges, but in future, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I come from a jurisdiction where that is taken for granted. We always say it, even when we finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We say sometimes good afternoon, sometimes good evening, sometimes good night, depending on what time we finish. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman. I appear with Tania Radosavljevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, it's Maitre Pitron, assisted by Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I almost did not recognise you, Maitre Pitron. I had almost forgotten how you looked. I understand, before we rose yesterday, last thing was something that you mentioned, which the Trial Chamber basically is very grateful that you raised. And that is the -- when you remarked that Mr. Ackerman had failed during his cross-examination to ask Mr. Smailagic any questions with regard to his statement that he had heard Mr. Brdjanin on one or more occasions state that the population of Muslims in Banja Luka would be reduced, would have to be reduced, ideally to between 3 and 5 per cent. The issue being, of course, what practice ought to be -- what will be the practice actually, because this is of course the first time that we are meeting, you're coming from one jurisdiction; I'm coming from another. Mr. Ackerman is coming from another, and the French team is coming from another jurisdiction. And I frankly myself did not realise that this would be an issue and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that you raised it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I explain? I think perhaps if I can just explain why. Firstly, a rule, it's a relatively recent rule, but it was passed. Can I ask Your Honours to look at Rule 90(H)(ii)?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, where it states in cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case for the party for whom that counsel appears, which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness. Now, Your Honour, Mr. Smailagic, I think on at least two occasions mentioned that he'd heard Mr. Brdjanin say that no more than between 2 and 5 per cent of Muslims should remain in Banja Luka. That was one thing. And the second thing related to how Muslims were going to be treated, I think something to do with a shoe. I can't remember the exact words. Now, it's noteworthy that he was challenged, firstly, that Kupresanin had said the words, "who is not with us, who is against us," but that was left alone. Now, Your Honour, that's particularly important because the indictment - and it's a long time since we've all looked at it - in paragraph 16, in describing the individual criminal responsibility and superior authority of the accused Brdjanin, says, particularly at the sentence beginning, "As such from the early stages, he played a leading role in the takeover of power by the SDS in particular with respect to the propaganda campaign, which was an essential component of the SDS plan to create a Serbian state." Now, Your Honour, obviously one doesn't expect every single aspect which may be challenged by the accused, if he gives evidence, or on which you will be addressed at the end, to be put, but certainly, on major matters, we suggest that the Defence must put its case properly. Mr. Ackerman understands that because, as you saw, he also put his case clearly about the accused's membership of the SDS in Banja Luka. Your Honour, the reason for it, and I think I ought to make this clear, is we have a huge case with a large number of witnesses. We would like, obviously, to reduce the amount of evidence we have to call, and we are only put on notice as to what evidence is challenged by being challenged. We could have assumed that there was no challenge to the words that Mr. Smailagic heard, and therefore have not called evidence about it because we don't want to call unnecessary evidence. And so that is why, in our submission, it's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're perfectly right. Mr. Ackerman, let me hear what you have to say in regard, and then I will see what the Defence team for General Talic has to say and then I tell you my -- not my opinion but what our stand will be in the course of these proceedings. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue must begin with the Statute of the Tribunal, which always overrides any rule that the Judges may fashion. The Judges may only fashion rules that are in accordance with the Statute of the Tribunal which comes from the Security Council of the United Nations. That Statute requires -- has a number of matters regarding the rights of the defendant, and one of those rights is to have the Prosecutor prove the case against him beyond a reasonable doubt, to have the burden of proof always rest with the Prosecutor and never shift to the Defence. The interpretation which Ms. Korner wants you to put on Rule 90 would be an egregious violation of the Statute in that regard because what she is suggesting to you is that somehow she can prove her case by the silence of the Defence. And the silence of the Defence should never be a basis upon which she could prove her case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment, Mr. Ackerman. That's not how this Trial Chamber has understood what Ms. Korner has stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not. Let's start from here, two basic principles. Number one is that no one expects Defence counsel to be as thorough in the cross-examination as to cover the whole evidence in chief of the witness. Definitely, that is not the case. I mean, because otherwise you would be penalised if you miss one question, if you miss two questions, or if you miss the third question. That's not the point. The whole point is this: What is the position, this is what I would like to hear from you, if on a major issue on which the witness has been quite categoric upon being examined, what is the position if, upon cross-examination, that issue is completely ignored? In other words, if no questions are put to the witness to confront him with whatever in relation to that categoric statement on a major issue that he would have made before. This is what I want to hear from you. And I more or less, in order not to prolong it unduly, my personal opinion, basing myself on the principle that emerges from the Statute, that the burden of proof, that the onus of proof, never shifts on the Defence unless and except in certain limited areas and for certain limited purposes only. And secondly, the rule that Ms. Korner referred me -- made reference to, accompanied with other rules that govern examination-in-chief and cross-examination. Let's imagine for a moment that -- you may sit down and then when it's time -- let's imagine for a moment that witness Smailagic made an affirmation, which could be the affirmation that Ms. Korner referred to yesterday or it could be another one. In this particular case, the affirmation is that on more than one occasion, he heard your client, I think on TV or on the radio or in a square, make a statement to the effect that the plan is, the idea is, the desideratum is, that at the end of this story there will only be 2 to 5 per cent Muslims in the Banja Luka -- in the Banja Luka municipality. Now, that is something which definitely, as Ms. Korner explained, falls within the parameters of a very specific accusation that is being levelled against your client. The position as this Tribunal sees it is as follows: A statement has been made by a witness. A statement has been made by a witness. Question number one, does it need to be contradicted by the Defence in the course of the cross-examination of that witness? Number one. And in that regard, it seems that Rule 90(H)(ii) or 90(H) seems to imply that in cross-examining the witness, the Defence ought to challenge that witness on what it thinks can be challenged. But let's say that you forget or you decide it's not wise or it's -- it will not be useful or sometimes it may be counterproductive to you to put the question, especially anticipating that you will get a second confirmation by the witness of that statement. Now, this Tribunal, as composed, can assure you that we are aware of these dangers. I mean, I was taught when I was still a very young lawyer to be careful what questions to put, especially upon cross-examination, because sometimes you ask a question and the chances are that if you ask that question, you go back home worse off than you were at the beginning of the day. So you are, most of the time, very careful. The whole point is this: At the end of the exercise, because this is not just an exercise which implies the evidence of Mr. Smailagic, but it is an exercise which implies a terrific, a humungous amount of evidence, what will be situation be? Now, if the situation will be that on day 19 and day 18 of February, 2002, witness Zijahudin Smailagic heard Mr. Brdjanin say on two occasion the words that were made reference to, were referred to earlier on, and if we also find on record that a week earlier, Mr. Muharem Krzic said exactly the same thing, and in both instances the two witnesses were not challenged as regards these statements, and in the course of the trial, no evidence was forthcoming which puts those statements in doubt, then obviously the fact that you did not cross-examine that witness on that particular point is going to have a bearing. It's going to carry some weight. So in reality, what I am -- what I am telling you before I hear you, and I am doing this precisely to help you and the Defence team for General Talic come forward on this, I think that first we ought to be grateful to Ms. Korner for having raised the issue yesterday, because I realised afterwards that it would have been most unfair if we were to go ahead with this trial and you not knowing what the position would be. And therefore I personally, also on behalf of my two colleagues, am very grateful to Ms. Korner for her loyalty to you and to the Trial Chamber in raising this matter. That's number one. Secondly, I think we ought to have this cleared out as we are not here to do the job of anyone here, neither of the Prosecution nor of the Defence, nor are we being asked to do it. But this is a long trial, Mr. Ackerman. This is going to be a long, long trial. I spent hours already with my legal staff and with my two Judges, trying to organise ourselves as from day one in a way which would make it relatively easy for us, certainly not impossible to reach our conclusions and to do our work well when we come to the crux later on, maybe in a year and a half's time or maybe even later. You are more or less in the same position. The fact that you may not have asked questions to Mr. Smailagic on this point and the fact that this is not mentioned at all between now and when we come to the final pleadings, coupled with perhaps a few other instances that we may come across later on, because I would imagine that this is not the only instance where this is going to happen, maybe damning, and this is where I am being frank with you and I'm trying to open the eyes. The Rule 90(H) is there for a reason, because just as there are rules governing cross-examination, what ought to be included or what should be included in a cross-examination and what should be left out, these are very important rules, because it's not a question of drawing an inference from the silence of the Defence. You've put it wrongly. It's a question of having a piece of evidence, a statement, made by a witness, which may end up being or remaining uncontradicted. If it is contradicted later on by other evidence, you don't have to worry about it. But it may well be that it will not be contradicted because you will forget about it the first time, you will forget about it the second or the third time, and the French team of lawyers will forget about it, too. No one remembers it, but at the end of the day, we are going to have it the way we are operating, this Trial Chamber with our legal team. At the end of every evidence, the basic points are being catalogued. So at the end of the day, if there is a cross-reference by a future witness, et cetera, it goes straight -- by way of a cross-reference to previous statements by others. So I think I suggest to you -- let me hear what you have to say. But I'm sure you have understood the approach of this Trial Chamber in regard to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, I understand what you're saying. The thing that I thought I heard Ms. Korner saying was that by my failure to ask him about that one particular statement, that the issue was foreclosed forever and she had proved that point, and that I would not even be able to put on evidence to contradict it. If that's the case, then I think it's a gross violation of the Statute. It seems to me that it's of no value to the Trial Chamber or anyone else for me to say to a witness, "Isn't it true you lied about Mr. Brdjanin making that statement" so that he can say, "No, I didn't; it's true," so you hear it twice. What does that do for you and what does that do for me? Nothing. It just prolongs cross-examination. Now, I can extend my cross-examinations - which I think already you think are too long - by another hour or two, to make sure I cover every point, and I don't think that's what you're asking me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to cover every point, but the question has been put very bluntly and in no uncertain terms by Ms. Korner to you. When you failed or when you decided - because it's not a question of you failed - when you opted against putting that question to Mr. Smailagic, does it mean to say that you are no longer contending that Mr. Brdjanin on one or two occasions made that statement? You should -- I think it's perfectly legitimate for Ms. Korner, and I would do the same, to ask that question, because I would definitely want to know which position you are putting, because if you are putting me in a position whereby you are agreeing that that statement is not being contested, then obviously I don't need to bring forward any other evidence, but if you leave it pending like that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once you are asked, because if you are not asked, no one is going to force you to put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But don't blame Ms. Korner for having raised the matter. Because if she has a duty, as she has, of regulating her case, bringing forward all the necessary -- don't forget that the Prosecution, like you, have got not just the onus of the burden of proof, which you don't have, but they also have the duty of bringing forward the best evidence, and the best evidence means that if a point, an issue, is contested, then if they have four, five, six witnesses that can prove that point, until they are and unless they are directed, stop, that's enough, they have a duty to bring forward that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, I mean, the spirit which motivated Ms. Korner I think is highly laudable. She is saying, "I am trying to make the life of everyone here as easy as possible and not to prolong the proceedings unduly by bringing forward unnecessary witnesses. Does the fact that you failed to put these questions while Rule 90(H) would otherwise require you to put a question in contradiction to the statement, does it mean that you are not contesting that part of the statement?" Of course she is right in asking that question of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the time comes when I make admissions of various allegations in parts of the indictment, I will make it extraordinarily clear that that's what I'm doing. I won't do that sneakily in any way. The other thing that Your Honours must understand, and Ms. Korner wants to even put on a witness to tell you about how these statements are taken, but what you must understand is like this witness, when he did his direct examination, we heard a number of things for the first time that are not in his statement, and I'm not speaking of the particular matter that she raised but a number of things he said here for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's going to happen with every witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's going to happen with every witness, and to expect me to immediately stand up and have the evidence to back a question like Ms. Korner suggests I should ask, is just too much. All I can do is, when I hear him say something that has never been in a statement, that I've never heard before, is ask my people in Banja Luka to begin investigating that. Now, I take it with regard to the issue that we are talking about that I will be permitted, and I'm sure you've made this clear to me, if I choose to, to bring as many witnesses as you will let me bring who were present at that rally at which he says Mr. Brdjanin said this, to say, "I was there and he did not say it." That would be a way for me to contest it and I think the proper way for me to contest it. Any other way would probably violate the Statute. The other thing, in my country, and I assume this is true, it has been here before, if a witness testifies falsely before this Tribunal about an important matter, the Tribunal then has the option to reject his entire testimony. That's an instruction we give to juries in the United States and I take it that if a witness on cross-examination, if I spend 15 minutes and prove him a liar on three matters, I could sit down and rest on the proposition that I've proven him to be a liar and that you should not credit anything that he said. That would certainly save time but if -- and I don't think I should have to go through every statement that every witness makes and figure out some way to contradict it. It would be dishonest, among other things, because I can't legitimately ask a witness a question that I haven't even investigated the issue about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, before I ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I reply to that before you here so that I deal with Mr. Ackerman's points in order? The first is this: The requirement, and I emphasise it, the requirement in the Rules, and it is no good Mr. Ackerman saying that any rule that is in conflict with the Statute must be struck down. There has been, as I understand it, no appeal against this Rule. It is there, and the Rules are there for a reason, and historically, as I understand it, one of the reasons it was put in was because exactly what Mr. Ackerman has described was happening, that when the Defence put on its case, suddenly a whole major aspect of the Prosecution case was challenged which had never been put to any of the witnesses. The reason it is there is not to require the Defence to prove anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But merely to put to the witness so that Your Honours can see, amongst other things, the reaction of the witness, because you have to assess, when there is a conflict of evidence, whether or not you are satisfied so that you are sure the Prosecution witness or the Defence witness, whichever it -- no, really the Prosecution witness, has told you the truth. And so therefore the reaction of the witness is an important aspect of the assessment of the evidence. Mr. Ackerman is perhaps -- I'm not sure what the right word is -- but it's absolutely clear that he understood the rule and applied the rule, because as I said to Your Honour, he put to Mr. Smailagic that at no stage did -- was Mr. Brdjanin a member of the Banja Luka SDS. He put to him that he was wrong in one of the things that he said. The one thing that he's not put, and I understand why he hasn't put it, he doesn't want to put his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a second? You are so right, Ms. Korner. If you look at the French text, I purposely -- I suppose you are all in possession of this document, a compilation of articles of the rules and how they have developed from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think -- actually, I don't think I am but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you look at the French text of this rule, it is very clear. In other words, what it says, [French spoken - no interpretation]. In other words, if you have -- you have a duty in cross-examination, cross-examining the witness, to confront him with information, with facts, that you know of, and which contradict his statement. In other words, the rule itself makes it compulsory on whoever is conducting the cross-examination, because it would work both ways, if there has been a statement and you are in possession of facts which contradict that statement, you must put those facts to the witness by way of showing him that there is evidence which contradicts him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, may I just finish before Mr. Ackerman replies? Because the points that he's just made about witnesses saying that things which are not in their statements, now, Your Honour, we appreciate that and particularly with the older statements, witnesses have a great deal more to say and when the witnesses are proofed, if they say something new, the Defence is supplied as much as possible with what else they are going it talk about so they can take instructions. But the answer is if a witness in the witness box says something directly pertinent to the defendant or the defendant's case which he has not said before, then the defendant is sitting there and nobody could object if time is asked to take instructions from the defendant on that new aspect. So, Your Honour, I just wanted to add that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've just raised another way, Your Honour, how this rule if interpreted the way you've suggested is in gross violation of the Statute, and that's this, and Ms. Korner just said it. We give you information far enough in advance to take instructions. What she means by saying that is that if a witness says that Mr. Brdjanin did something, that I'm supposed to go ask him and come back and tell you what he said, which is a gross violation of his right to remain silent. And I will not do that. I can't do that. That's a violation of my ethics to report to this Court what he told me in confidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To do it in the form of asking a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I would invite you -- that's beside the point I think at this point. I would invite you to look, if you understand French, to look at the French version of this rule because it is a far cry from being a literal translation of the English version. The English version is, "shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears, which is in contradiction of the evidence of the witness." The French version literally translated means or should read, "You have a duty to confront that witness with the -- those elements or those facts about which you are -- which you have at your disposal which contradict his statement." So there is a conflict between -- according to me, not a conflict, they certainly do not say the same thing, and the French version certainly gives much more sense to what -- Ms. Korner's position than the English translation itself. It's certainly more categoric. If you want to see it, I have it here available. I can let you see it. But I suppose you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would have access to it. I wouldn't be able to read it with the precision that you can, Your Honour, or my colleagues behind me. And that then raises the question of whether there is one rule or two rules because if they are that dramatically different, then there are two rules and then which one controls?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The aim is that basically since the cross-examination is a -- taking the witness to task on what he stated in examination, in the examination-in-chief, this is the whole purpose of the cross-examination. Basically, if you are moving outside of those parameters, you can only do it with the permission of the Court. But within those parameters, you're taking the witness to task. It should be complete, as complete an exercise as possible, with the consequence that, although you do not have the onus of proof shifted on you at any given time, no one is saying that, neither did Ms. Korner say that the onus of proof is shifted on you upon cross-examination of the witness, no one said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just close this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want the record to be clear that I am asserting at this point that if Rule 90(H)(i) is applied in the way that Ms. Korner suggests --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, 90(H)(ii), Roman II, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- is applied in the way Ms. Korner is suggesting that it violates the Statute of this Tribunal in the ways that I have said. Secondly, I must now request that I be permitted to reopen my cross-examination of Mr. Smailagic and so that I can go through all these matters with him that Ms. Korner suggests that I should have initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose first you would agree that we finish with the cross-examination of Mr. Smailagic by the team for General Talic. Now, do Maitre Pitron or Madam Fauveau have anything to say on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the issue that you have raised is interesting because it does illustrate the differences of our procedure. The questions that you have raised don't seem to be raised in an inquisitional system or, if so, it's in a very different manner because the proof would have been brought before the beginning of the trial, the evidence. We are talking about existing evidence, and not about evidence that appears in the course of the examination. So although General Talic is not concerned by this particular point, by this factual point, the legal issue is interesting in itself. I think that we should refer to the text, which is what you have done, and rightly so. My interpretation is not quite the same as yours, of Article 90(H)(ii). What I notice in the second part of the sentence in this article is that the party who is cross-examining the witness has to confront him with the elements that they have which are in contradiction of his statement. And as a cross-examiner, I have to challenge the witness's statement with evidence that I have at my disposal. Yes, I have to do that. But I have to challenge him on the basis of the elements that I dispose of, and if I have understood problem that we are faced with, Mr. Ackerman had no such evidence in order to respond to the witness's statement, because in the witness's statement, written statement, which was a basis on which the cross-examination was prepared, the reference to the two declarations that Mr. Brdjanin made was non-existent. So this is a new element which appears in the debate. How can the Defence respond to elements that it had no information on? So as far as this question is concerned, I think that it is possible to provide three cumulative answers. The first answer is that it is normal for the witness to be re-examined again on a new point and that the cross-examination be reopened after the Defence has been able to analyse the witness's new statements and to discuss this with its client. My second remark is that the witness -- I'm sorry, the Defence, may always, if it so desires in the course of the trial, either by cross-examining a witness or by presenting its own witnesses, they can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. raise a new debate on questions in order to clarify matters. And the last remark I would like to make, and I'm referring to the inquisitional system, in any event, the Defence's final argument provides a summary of its position. And after my argument, I contest what the witness says, even something that he said a few months earlier, I think that your Tribunal has to take account that I'm against the statement that the witness made that I don't agree with it, even if in this particular case, I only -- I only have my word and I have no other evidence to provide. So in conclusion, I think that if we follow this line of reasoning, we will be respecting a fundamental principle which transcends the Rules of the Tribunal, the Rules of Evidence of the Tribunal and all the other principles that have to be applied in all trials. This is the principle of contradiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can we close the matter here? More or less, the position as the Trial Chamber sees it is as follows: This is not a question of whether when winding up the case at the final stages, you have a right or not to say, "We don't agree with this. We don't agree with that. We submit that this has not been proven. We submit that there is reasonable doubt on this and a reasonable doubt on that." This is not an issue. No one should even think for a moment that this will not take place when the time comes. The whole issue is this: May I please remind you, in my career as a Judge I have lost count, and I wouldn't even try to count the number of judgements which I wrote in which my conclusions are based on the facts that certain statements made by witnesses in the course of the proceedings remain unchallenged, uncontradicted. It's not a question of you standing up and saying, "We do not agree with this. We don't agree with that." At the end of the day, whoever is going to decide on the facts is going to put in the basket all the evidence that has been forthcoming, pro and con, and see what the situation is. If there is a fact that has been stated on oath or under solemn declaration, even once if necessary, which is capable of being believed, and the Trial Chamber believes it, and that fact especially is not contradicted, the fact that it is not contradicted is going it carry a tremendous weight. This is why, rather than confronting Ms. Korner on -- for having raised the matter, I'm thankful to her, because it has made things clear to more or less to everyone, especially since we come from different jurisdictions. I'm fully aware of the difficulty that this may cause, especially for someone coming from the continental system, like the French or the Italian or the -- the Spanish or the Portuguese, or even the German and even the Dutch, if I remember well. But the thing is this, we are not saying that a fact stated by a witness upon examination-in-chief, if not contradicted in the course of that cross-examination -- of the cross-examination, can never be contradicted afterwards. What we are saying is that you have a duty under 90(H)(ii) to confront that witness with any elements, any facts that are in your possession which are in contradiction with his statement. The basic conclusion, the logical conclusion, legal conclusion - because I'm not interested in syllogisms here - the legal conclusion, Mr. Ackerman and Maitre Pitron, is and can only be, if what I told you now is valid, in other words, that at the end of the day the fact that something has not been contradicted will carry -- will have a bearing, will carry its proper weight. It will carry an even greater weight if you had, possibly, information that you could have faced that witness with and you never faced that witness with that information. It's not a question of you being prejudiced because you prevailed yourself or took advantage of the benefit you have to remain silent. This is not the case. There is a rule which makes it imperative that you should confront a witness upon cross-examination with evidence that you may have which should -- which can be used to contradict him or which shows him at least that you are not accepting his statement. In this particular case, telling him, "I am in possession of -- I have witnesses that are prepared to give evidence here that you're not saying the truth," for the purpose of this exercise under 90(H)(ii) would probably suffice, but you have to face it under 90(H)(ii), in other words, not leave it, let it pass by as if it's not being contested by you. Are we there? Not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a good thing I sleep a full eight hours every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm glad you do. I wish I could. There are two more matters, I guess, that I need to bring to your attention in light of this. The first thing, I think the Prosecution will agree with me, I've cursorily looked, and I'm pretty sure I'm correct, that in none of the statements of Mr. Smailagic did he report, even after four days of questioning by OTP investigators, that Mr. Brdjanin had ever said, "We would keep between 3 and 5 per cent of balijas here to make them do humiliating jobs, the jobs which were humiliating for Serbs." No where in his statements does this appear. And, all of a sudden, my failure to contest it is taken as some kind of an admission, and I think that's not correct. The other thing that I now need to report to Your Honours because of what I've been hearing just the last few moments is this: At about 10.00 last night, I received some additional new documents from Banja Luka that were discovered in the course of the further investigation of the things this witness has said. I concluded last night that it was -- it would just be extraordinarily time consuming and delaying for me to try to get those in the position they could be used as exhibits and ask you to let me continue my cross-examination of this witness to get them translated, to do all the things necessary to use them. But if you're going to apply a rule which says I must confront him with things as to which I have knowledge, then I would ask that we -- that we take some time, that we have a short recess, 30 minutes to 45 minutes, so that I can get these materials prepared as exhibits, so that I can be assisted by my staff to understand better the contents of them and then be able to question him about them. I will tell you that they have to do with his contentions regarding this travel agency and Perka, and who owned it and who operated it, and I think we have documents that now make it quite clear that virtually everything he said about that agency is wrong and incorrect and untrue. My idea was to get them translated and marked and give them to the Prosecutor as reciprocal discovery within the next couple of days, but not to use them until there was perhaps an appropriate witness to use them with, that the Prosecutor would call or with a witness that I would call later in the case. So I'm now at a position where I must ask the Chamber what you would prefer that I do with regard to these new documents and I will do what you suggest, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, a very quick answer to that. I don't -- I think that what we have been discussing so far has been the result of an issue that was brought up by Ms. Korner and which was limited only to a very particular part of the evidence of Mr. Smailagic. That is the part in which he specifically alleged to have heard your client say the words that we mentioned before. And I think we ought at this stage to limit ourselves to that issue, with the understanding that - which probably you have understood already - that you will have an opportunity once we finish with the cross-examination by the team of General Talic, to re-examine -- re-cross-examine or reopen your cross-examination of Mr. Smailagic with regard to that point. There is no allegation that you have failed to observe the dictates of Rule 90(H)(ii) with regard to any other point, aspect, of Mr. Smailagic's evidence. With regard to this particular issue, the agency, Perka, whether Perka is Mr. Brdjanin's wife, was there an involvement by Mrs. Brdjanin in this agency, was there an involvement by Mr. Brdjanin in this agency, or not, I think you confronted Mr. Smailagic with the evidence that you had there, obtained from him, an affirmation that Perka was not Mr. Brdjanin's wife, that this agency was not run by Mr. Brdjanin's wife but by this Perka and by Mr. Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Glogovac, and I can now prove that's not true, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I think you can prove that and you will obviously have all the facility to prove that later on when it's your turn to prove anything, if I am using the correct term, and I don't think we should raise it up now to reopen a chapter that I consider closed. Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I remind Mr. Ackerman he doesn't have to prove anything at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I said if I'm using the correct words.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of the 2 per cent aspect, we absolutely accept that those words were not in Mr. Smailagic's statement. However, this is an aspect of the case that appears in a number of witnesses' statements and at one stage was actually specifically stated in the indictment. It was removed on one of the amendments because it was evidence, so it's not something Mr. Ackerman can say he was unaware of that this was part of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also mentioned by the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Your Honour, so far as that is concerned, we agree with Your Honour. We are not asking for the aspect of Perka. Mr. Ackerman did put his case quite clearly. He doesn't accept what Mr. Smailagic says. The only thing I would mention is this business of documents suddenly arriving from Banja Luka, all the evidence about the Perka agency was contained in those statements. So Mr. Ackerman did know well in advance. So I'm somewhat troubled by this question of documents suddenly arriving. However, for these purposes, Your Honour, all we are asking is that Mr. Ackerman put to Mr. Smailagic, if that is his case, that these words were not used by Mr. Brdjanin. That is with respect to the 2 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how this Trial Chamber sees it, anyway. Okay? We should only be restricted to this. So I think we can call in the witness now. I hope he's been offered a coffee or something while he has been waiting. Yes, Madam Fauveau, wait before you bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness comes, I would like to apologise on behalf of Maitre de Roux and ask you for permission to continue with the cross-examination that he started yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that you have the full trust and confidence of General Talic. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you can remain standing while the witness is brought in, and you can proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Smailagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The gentleman next to you is going to hand you the same document in which there is a solemn declaration that you are kindly asked to read out to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. If you look to your left, you will see a lady lawyer standing, who will be putting questions to you. This is a continuation of the cross-examination by the Defence team of General Talic that was started yesterday shortly before we finished the sitting. Madam Fauveau will be putting some questions to you. Yes, please proceed, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before starting, the two statements -- could the two statements, the witness's two statements be provided to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smailagic, do you have copies of your statements in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. I've received them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Ms. Fauveau-Ivanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Smailagic, Maitre de Roux asked you a series of questions yesterday regarding your activities in 1992. I'm going to continue with this series of questions. Yesterday, you said that when you informed the international organisations, the authorities and the -- and the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the situation in Banja Luka, you were playing a political and humanitarian role. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not just a humanitarian role. We were politically engaged as representatives of a certain people, group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you played a role which was political and humanitarian?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were being examined on the 19th of February, 2002, you said that you hadn't received any military information.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't gather any. But we didn't ask, we didn't seek to gather any. We didn't take any action. It was just citizens who would come, because they didn't have anyone else to address in Banja Luka apart for us. And then we would find out this information and we would forward it, regardless of the nature of that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you confirm that among the information that you received, there was also military information?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could consider it to be such, as it was a military -- everything was under the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that there was military information that you received?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the information you are referring to. We were only interested in, because there were quite a few Muslims and Croats who were forced to -- to be mobilised. They were taken to the front, to the battlefield. And that's what interested us most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about certain information which concerns the Serbian army's attacks or information concerning Serbian soldiers who were killed at the front.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was such information too, perhaps something about attacks, and perhaps something about wounded, how many were brought into Banja Luka, because we could hear this from the Serbs themselves. There were quite a few people from Banja Luka of Serbian nationality; they were in the army. Someone would be wounded from someone's family and that's how we would find out this. And then -- but nothing special was organised to gather information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that some of the faxes that you received or sent were coded.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't know what the coded ones were about and I didn't ask what they were about. Maybe there were two or three of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact there were messages, the contents of which were unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't know. Later I found out, after the war, that these messages were of a private nature sometimes, and so on. But the real contents of these messages, no, I never found out what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that among these coded messages, there were some which contained military information?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't make a comment on that because I said I didn't know what the content of these messages was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to address another subject. Yesterday, you said that many Serbs fled from Croatia and came to Bosnia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was about 1991. They were civilians, mostly old people. There were some young people but they were mostly old people and women, and they were refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at your statement of the year 2001? I think it's the statement number 2. On page 3, you also said that many Serbs fled from Croatia and from different regions in Bosnia. The first paragraph on page 3, the middle of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, if you have the B/C/S version in front of you, perhaps you could direct him better, because I'm sure it will not be the first paragraph on page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the first paragraph, the first entire paragraph, which starts with the phrase, with the words, [In English] "The meeting was held."

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree that you said there were many Serbs who fled from different areas in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the first time they started arriving, they were mostly from Slavonia or Posavena, Pakrac, Novo Gradiska, that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, but it is the region of Bosnia that I'm interested in. Could you tell us from which areas of Bosnia these Serbs fled from?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later they came from Travnik, I think, and from Jajce, too. That's more or less the situation. And then later on, we didn't even know where they were coming from because there were quite a lot of refugees in Banja Luka then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why these Serbs fled from their regions and came to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because of the war, there was -- there was fighting there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at a hearing that the SDA party was a multi-ethnic party in the start, the hearing on the 19th of February.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that some Serbs were members of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because of their security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we were in closed session and the information was confidential in such a case, would you provide us with their names?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said during the same hearing that some Croats were members of the SDA before the formation of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the HDZ had been founded, did a certain number of Croats remain in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They said thank you to us and they joined the HDZ party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Serbs who were members of the SDA, what was their fate?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They simply withdrew in silence, they didn't appear any more. There was no sense in asking them to come to us, because there was fear and we were afraid, as were the Croats and the Serbs were afraid too, because there were quite a few Serbs who thought in a slightly different way. If you have a look at the text of the decision on earlier relations, you will see in one part it says, the Serbs who didn't turn up at the plebiscite, there were quite a few Serbs who didn't respond to the plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the elections in 1990, were there still Serbs and Croats or that is Serbs, in the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the elections, at the time of the elections, no. They were registered when the party was -- they were registered then but they weren't active participants. They were members, though, and that was known. Before the elections, and during the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the elections were held, the SDA party was already a party which had a homogeneous national membership?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that when these elections were held, there were left parties, the SDP and reformists, which had a multi-national composition?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's true. They were the reformist forces, the League of Communists, the movement for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that the list of candidates for these parties was also multi-national?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that now, believe me, I really can't. I couldn't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be given the document DB31, the Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's one of the documents exhibited by you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is correct, Madam Fauveau, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it's a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is the official bulletin of the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think maybe he's only been given the English version and I think there is also a B version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see from here, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a B version. It was specifically given to the Registrar on Friday. So it's somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to save time, we were given a B version so the witness can have ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you agree that this is the official bulletin of the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that this official bulletin contains the electoral list of various parties for the elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at page 5? There is a list of the candidates of the Reformist Party.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see that among these candidates there are people of various nationalities, of all the nationalities?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among the candidates, there are Yugoslavs, too?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was a difference between Muslim and non-Muslim names, and that one could tell whether a person was a Muslim on the basis of that person's name and surname.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at this list and tell us if the majority of Yugoslavs here are Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the Yugoslavs Slavs here I would have to count them now --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to help you, Mr. Smailagic. The person under number 6, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person is Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this person's name a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Person number 8?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Person number 19?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that the person under number 22 could be said to be -- could be said to have a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Person number 28?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would certainly agree that the person number 30 and 31 could be Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Person number 37, is this person a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name isn't Muslim but the surname is a Muslim surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you couldn't state that this person is a Muslim, you couldn't confirm this?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but listen, on what basis is this confirmed? On the basis of the name of the father and of the mother. We would then have to establish this, because there were names after the Second World War. We would even give people names such as Goran, Zlatko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person is a woman?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agree that women in Bosnia changed their names after they have been married?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm talking about Banja Luka. There were quite a few mixed marriages in Banja Luka and it would be -- it might be possible that this woman was from a mixed marriage, that her father was a Muslim and her mother a Croatian or Serbian and then they agreed what sort of name they would give him. There were quite a few such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have a look at person number 51 now, is this a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 53?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 63; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it helps Madam Fauveau, she has made the point very clearly, and I think Your Honours have seen the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt her but I think you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We take the point very well, Madam Fauveau, and I'm sure the Judges do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the choice of nationality is a personal choice? It's something that is private?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this case, why were you -- why did you take the liberty of treating Muslims, of treating people who had declared themselves to be Yugoslavs as Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe the term Muslim, maybe the term is wrong. Muslims are people who -- whose religion is Islam but before the elections, and before the law was brought, according to which Muslims were recognised as a nation, it was possible to declare yourself as a Serb, a Croat, or not to declare yourself, and this wasn't clear with all the people. And later, the category of Yugoslav was introduced. And when "undeclared," the undeclared category was withdrawn, then it was possible to declare yourself as a Yugoslav. I think that on one occasion, I said that the Muslims, not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina but also in Yugoslavia, the category of Yugoslav was the one that they favoured the most. And many people opted for this category. And some followed Mr. Ante Markovic. But this did not bother us because we wanted to see exactly how many Muslims there were, on the basis of their religion, on the basis of Islam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say 52.000 Muslims in Banja Luka, you're talking about people whose religion is Islam but not whose nationality is Muslim, so today we would say people of Bosniak nationality?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will need to break in a few minutes' time, so you choose the time when you prefer to stop and then of course you will resume Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. afterwards. If you have a few more questions now, you have got about three, four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer to stop now because I'm going to start on another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will break for 20, 25 minutes, resuming at ten to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Bring the witness in, please. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness, so I don't forget to do it later, we have now provided the Registry with the B/C/S versions of the documents that we submitted yesterday, 44 and 45, and I would therefore move admission of the exhibits that I've used with this witness, which would be 42A and 43 through 45, A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Yes, Mr. Smailagic, Madam Fauveau will be proceeding with her cross-examination of you. And I wish to advise you also that when her cross-examination ends, there are a couple of further questions that the Trial Chamber is authorising Mr. Ackerman, counsel for Mr. Brdjanin, to make to you, or to put to you. So you will be cross-examined further by Mr. Ackerman, and then there will be time for re-examination, if it is the case, and we take it up from there and see whether there are questions that the Trial Chamber itself would like to put to you. Madam Fauveau, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 22nd of February, 2002, the hearing of that date, during your examination, you said that Celinac and Laktasi was part of the municipality of Banja Luka during a certain period?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that leaving this municipality, when this municipality left the municipality of Banja Luka, was done in order to change the structure of the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the ethnic structure of Celinac and Laktasi was mixed?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say what percentage of Muslims lived in Celinac?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact percentage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Laktasi?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact percentage in Laktasi. I know for the village of Mahovljani, which was almost exclusively populated by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar give the witness the document D1?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, it's DT1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need a further copy here. Do you have any further copies? Because we are short of one copy here. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, do you agree that these are the results of the census, of the population census?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at page 2 of this document? It's the percentage of the population on the basis of nationality. If you have a look at number 7, you have Celinac there. Could you tell us what the percentage of Serbs was in Celinac?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 88.9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the percentage of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7.7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at number ten? It's the municipality of Laktasi. What was the percentage of Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 81.7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the percentage of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1.7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us now how come, when this commune left the municipality of Banja Luka, how could it influence in a negative way the number of Muslims in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you understood the question, Mr. Smailagic? Because I haven't. Could you rephrase it, perhaps, in a more clear way, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree that this municipality has a majority of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the fact that this municipality is no longer, was no longer part of the municipality of Banja Luka, how did this fact influence the number of Muslims in Banja Luka? How did it affect the number of Muslims in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, by leaving, when Laktasi left, Laktasi was not a municipality. Other villages joined and these villages, the population was exclusively Serbian. The same thing happened in Celinac, where Serbian villages joined. They joined Celinac. It wasn't a municipality. Whereas before this census, before 1991, that is to say when they were part of Banja Luka, then Celinac was quite different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the first page of this document? There is a number of persons there of Serbian nationality, of Muslim and Croatian nationality in Celinac. Could you say how many Muslims were there in Celinac?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Laktasi?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you agree that this is not a significant number?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a very important number here, but, look, what's important is what I wanted to say, that by -- when these municipalities left, Krupa na Vrbasu joined Banja Luka, Prozani [phoen] and Mahovljani, and also Ivanjska. I don't know if we mentioned this. It was a separate municipality. In Ivanjska, the Croatian population was in the majority and it joined the municipality of Banja Luka. So that's what changed the situation in Banja Luka, In the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agree that in the municipality Celinac and Laktasi, they have -- they had a Serbian majority, a vast Serbian majority?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that is the case, yes. Then in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day before yesterday, you mentioned people who had changed their names?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that most of these persons were women?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them were women. According to the information we had, yes, there were quite a few women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you a question a while ago, but I didn't receive a clear answer. Do you agree that in Bosnia, women would change their names when they got married?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the majority of cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try, as much as you can, not to repeat questions, because you put this question to him earlier on, before the break. And he gave you the same answer he's giving you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that these persons who changed their names were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was talking about Muslims who changed their names at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serbs change their names too?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that certain Muslims changed their names but they took other Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That wouldn't be a change then.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar provide the witness with the Prosecution's Exhibit P35 -- 135?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, it's a document that you saw yesterday, the official registration certificate of people who had changed their names. On the first page, you can see about 30 names. In the first column, would you agree that most of these names are Serbian names? It's on the first page, Mr. Smailagic.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page? That's right. Page 1, Elvir Delimehic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it's the page that starts with a change of personal name.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no page. It's the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, please let's make it simpler. The document which I have in front of me, that is Prosecution document P135, has got the first page, which has got very little information on it. The second page, the same. And then the first page with real details has as the first name, Elvir Delihramic. We start from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently the Prosecution has not given us the same document in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this is why, because I was getting confused myself. I imagine that Madam Fauveau knew what she was talking about. At the same time, I couldn't follow myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, the witness didn't look at this yesterday. I waived it, I think, generally, at Your Honour's saying here is the document about change of names, and I explained that what we had done -- because it's just a list of names, all we have done is translated what the top of the column is and then selected a few of the entries. Not all of it is translated. But it is a list of registered name changes, but the full document is only in the B/C/S language; only parts have been translated as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the reference number, the exhibit number of one and the other?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The exhibit number, it should say its disclosure number will be 1.112 but it's been premarked with Exhibit number P135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that would be this document which is a selected -- selection from the totality of the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that document, has it been exhibited or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, because it wasn't actually shown. It's been premarked but you have not formally admitted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You brought it over yesterday or the day before. You did show it to us, however, and we did show it to a witness. I think that's the document that we showed him yesterday, asking him whether that was the document to which he was referring as existing in this archive that he wouldn't tell us more about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. You're absolutely right. It came up and it was shown during the course of Mr. Ackerman's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was shown that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He said he didn't recognise that. And in fact it doesn't come -- it was seized - I can tell Your Honour in a moment - from the CSB building in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's see if we can make sense out of it. Madam Fauveau, are you making use of the full document at the present moment or are you making use of the selected, the selection from the list, which is marked as Exhibit P135?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will use the document in Serbo-Croat, which is complete, and I am just going to use the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think what is important to know is the witness's answer in any case, because you will be referring to names, I would suppose, no? But it is important, Ms. Korner, that this document is introduced in the records as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour has already admitted it because, Your Honour, it was part of the Banja Luka collection of documents and Your Honour has already formally admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is its exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P135 is the selected one. It's numbered P135 here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. No, Your Honour. The actual, the original document and the translation are normally exhibited together. This is P135A but it's a selective translation because in order to save the Translation Unit, about which more will be said later by both Mr. Ackerman and myself, we only asked for a selection of names to be translated because it's just a list of names. But the two documents are together. It's just that it's not a full translation. It's a selective translation. But one is P135A, the B/C/S version. The Serbo-Croat version is P135B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's important, Madam Registrar, that we have both, because as far as I'm concerned, I only have P135 without distinguishing whether it's A or B, and this would be A, and the other one would be B and we don't have it. We did see it yesterday, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the both versions, the English translation and the B/C/S, are in binder 1 of the Banja Luka binders which Your Honours have, but probably not in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So please -- I have two and three here because I only got the documents that were going to be referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have all of the binders with me and I took one P135 from the Banja Luka binder and I have -- that's the version that I've submitted to the witness. So I don't have the complete list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
