utterances.text: Anyway, Ms. Korner let's not waste time on it. Please, as usual, take it in hand later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will do this in the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Make sure that the position is regularised. Madam Fauveau, I'm sorry to have interrupted you but it was necessary. Please go ahead with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this the witness still doesn't have the right document. Could I ask for a pause, a ten minute pause, in order to make a photocopy of the document that the Prosecutor has provided us with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Ms. Korner will make hers available and that will solve the situation, the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I think the witness has got the B/C/S version, has he not? Yes, he has. So can I make it available to Your Honours at the moment, to share?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the first page where the first name is Mr. Zahirovic, Fadil? Zahirovic, Fadil?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have Zahirovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, could you kindly -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you kindly bring the document the witness has in front of him to me so that I double check that we are talking of the same document, and possibly even find the right page for him so that we don't waste more time? Again, this is not the complete document. The complete document that you gave me, Ms. Korner, or that you gave us, rather, starts from page 1. The document that the witness has starts from page 31. And he's being asked in relation to the first name that appears on page 1 of this list. So what I would suggest is that this is returned to the witness. For the time being, he ignores it. With your permission, Ms. Korner, I'm going to -- please, please -- I am going to give him the same document that you gave to us. We will be able to follow and then we will be able to double check later. And we can proceed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I see the registrar appears to have found the same document as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't matter that it's in English. The important thing is that it starts with page 1 and finishes with page 40 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What we will do is we will arrange for a number of copies to be made straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. In the meantime, I think we can proceed. It should be easy now for you to coordinate your efforts and finish this part of the cross-examination. Please proceed, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first person's name is Zahirovic, Fadil. That's his real name, the name he was born with?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what name this person changed his name to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Suljic here but there is no name and Suljic, and as far as I know, and I know this, was both a Serbian and -- there were both Serbs and Muslims with this surname, and there are quite a few surnames which belong to both nationalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that if the name does not -- if the surname does not appear, the first name is the same -- has remained the same?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at number 24? Mahmutovic, Zijaneta. It's a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She changed her name to Zijada?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Zijada a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 27, Krnic, Zarfa?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She changed her name to Zarafa?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 27, Moralic, Hasib?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He changed his name to Hasan?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that Hasan is a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, I don't know if you prefer to continue but I think you have made your point. The Trial Chamber doesn't think it's important to have further information on this point. It is obvious that some of these persons were changing -- actually one Muslim name with another Muslim name. So if you have any further points to make, please proceed. But otherwise, I would suggest that you move to your next question dealing with another subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question about the first names but it doesn't concern Muslims. It concerns the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the persons -- at the person under number -- at the persons under number 2 and 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 29 and 30?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that these persons are not Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that on this list, most of the persons who changed their names were Serbs or Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't distinguish this according to name. I can't distinguish who is a Serb and who is a Croat on the basis of the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move to another subject. On page 3 of your statement of the 15th of April, 2001, it's the first statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we give the statement to the witness, the one he made on the 15th of April? On page 3 of this statement, you said that the SDS no longer recognised the SDA as an official party and that this was in November 1991. It's the third paragraph, if you're looking at the end of the page -- from the end of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you found it, Mr. Smailagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you found the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't find it. I remember -- I can reply to the question in any case. They didn't officially stop the work of the party. The SDA -- SDA's work was never forbidden in Banja Luka, but on the basis of their behaviour, there was no more contact and later on they avoided contact. They ignored us, they didn't even want to talk to --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that the SDA stopped contacting you.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDA?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the SDS stopped contacting you.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had stopped contacting us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this happened in November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was around November. As far as I remember, there was a plebiscite in November. That's when these contacts --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that the only person on the SDA who continued going to the SDS meetings was Muharem Krzic.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his function was such, so he attempted to maintain certain contact to the extent that this was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his function?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you agree that the contact between the SDS and SDA continued after November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were not really meetings. It was always at the request of Mr. Krzic, with regard to what was happening in Banja Luka. In 1991, that's how things were developing then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the municipal assembly of Banja Luka continued working after November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal assembly of Banja Luka continued working but I know that our delegates from the municipal assembly were withdrawn. I can't exactly remember whether it was at the beginning of 1992 or towards the end of 1991. I really can't remember this now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, were there SDA deputies who continued going to the meetings of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was not the case, but as far as I can remember, one of those delegates, I think he remained in the parliament, and this was against the decision of the party. It was on his own initiative. Whether he was there regularly or not, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that this person was Emir Busatlic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a doctor, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Adem Gunic and Salko Hamdan, were they also SDA deputies?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they also continued in 1992 attending meetings of the municipal assembly? I mean after April.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Salko did not respect the decision made by the party that he should withdraw from the parliament, and Mr. Adem Gunic, I think he was the vice-president of the Banja Luka municipality and he wanted to keep his job, so he stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, you were a member of Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were active in the Merhamet of Banja Luka from 1991 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that Merhamet was a Muslim humanitarian organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you affirm that Merhamet was active throughout this period, from 1991 to 1994, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 5 of your first statement, the one made in the year 2000 - I think you have it here - you said that the curfew was imposed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a curfew was imposed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the curfew was intended for all citizens but, in fact, it was actually applied only to non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know it did not apply to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was very easy to discover because I could see my neighbours moving about from my window. They went out, they went to town in the evening without any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 5 of the same statement from the year 2000, you said that you heard that all Croats and all Muslims who did not respond to the call-up or for work duty were imprisoned in centres.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, whoever failed to respond to the call-up or to a summons to go to work duty, they were detained, I think either in a police station or in the basement of the Ministry of Defence. There they would spend the night. Some people were kept there two or three days, and then they were sent to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get this information about the arrest of non-Serbs who failed to respond to the call-up, and when you got this information, did you forward it either to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina or to some international organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both to the government and to the Red Cross and other international organisations, yes, we did forward this information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, personally, did you respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a draft notice, and I reported, but I brought with me my document showing that I was retired, and then I was sent to the Ministry of Defence, where I explained matters, and I was exempt from military duty and then I went home. Later on, I received a summons to respond to work duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you then respond to the summons? Did you do work duty?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday what happened. I went there with the document showing that I was disabled. Mr. Djuka did not want to accept this. He demanded that I bring --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question was very simple. Did you respond? Did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not go to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Muharem Krzic responded to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't be sure now. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was mobilised or not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, no, I never discussed it with him. If he was mobilised -- well, if he had been mobilised, I would have seen him in uniform. So I didn't see him in uniform before he left Banja Luka. Whether he got a draft notice, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Muharem Krzic did work duty?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you arrested in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Muharem Krzic, was he arrested in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was arrested in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question was only about the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, what you heard, that all non-Serbs who failed to respond to the call-up or to report for work duty were imprisoned in prison centres, this information was not correct, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean? You mean that they were detained? Some people in Banja Luka were detained in the police station. That was set up in the old army club, or in the basement of the building of the Ministry of Defence, or they went to the so-called small camp, where they spent the night. Some of them were detained there for two or three days and then they were taken to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will reformulate my question. Do you agree that in Banja Luka in 1992, there were persons who were not Serbs, who did not respond to the call-up, and who were not sent to do obligatory work? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not sent to do forced labour but perhaps they were given other duties or they left Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ackerman, I think it's time for you and for us to clear up the problem that we dealt with this morning. I would suggest to you to proceed with an additional cross-examination of the witness, limited to the point that we discussed. In other words, to the part of his testimony dealing with the statement that according to him he heard your client make on one or two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it is necessary, we can read to the witness the part of his testimony from his transcript or perhaps one could remind him of what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the transcript section found here in LiveNote and I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, any statements we would submit that relate to the attitude that Mr. Brdjanin, according to the witness, was showing towards non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You got the message, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we just expanded the horizon of my cross-examination rather dramatically, but I can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Smailagic, during your testimony of yesterday and the day before, there were some allegations made by you with regard to Mr. Ackerman's client, that is accused Radoslav Brdjanin. It has been agreed, and permission has been given to Mr. Ackerman to question you further about some of these statements of yours. Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, as we discussed yesterday, you, over the course of your statements to representatives of the OTP, you spent the date of 15 April, 2000, and 4 and 14 June, 2001, and 19 August, 2001, being questioned and answering those questions by investigators from the OTP, either all or parts of those dates. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during those sessions, the investigators from the OTP were asking you questions about matters in which they had an interest, and you were answering those questions. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the matters in which the investigators of the OTP were interested were Mr. Brdjanin and any statements you might have heard Mr. Brdjanin make, either on radio, television, speeches, that sort of thing, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in none of these sessions in 2000 and 2001, did you tell the investigators that you heard Mr. Brdjanin make a statement about 3 to 5 per cent balijas would be kept in Banja Luka and made to do humiliating jobs. You didn't ever say that in any of your statements to the OTP, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said that to the investigators or not, but I know it's true. They even mentioned 2 per cent, then they said 3 per cent, and then they said not more than 5 per cent. I could expand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My only question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Please try to answer Mr. Ackerman's questions. His clear question is a very clear one. He's referring to your statement, the second statement, that is the one made in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually both of them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But your question was more or less directed to this one: In which you do mention statements made by Mr. Brdjanin and others, meaning, according to Mr. Ackerman, that you were being asked as to whether you had heard such statements or statements forthcoming from Mr. Brdjanin and others, and you are being asked to explain whether you had specifically referred to the instance where Mr. Brdjanin, as you told us yesterday, and maybe others, mentioned that the number of Muslims in the Banja Luka municipality would eventually have to be reduced to either 2 or 3 or 5 per cent. Did you mention it to the investigators? This is his question. And the next one will be, if you didn't, why didn't you mention it? So you can answer both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I mentioned it or not. I think I did, but I'm not sure. If it's not in the statement, then probably I didn't. But the reason I didn't do so was that I wasn't asked. The question wasn't asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, you just told us that you were asked by the investigator from the OTP about statements you heard Mr. Brdjanin make. Now you're saying you weren't asked. Which one is the truth, Mr. Smailagic? Are you telling the truth the first time or the second time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not saying -- I'm just saying I don't remember whether the question was asked and whether I answered it or not. If it was asked, then I think I gave the same answer as I'm giving now. If it was not asked, if he didn't ask me this, then, well, I would have said so if I'd been asked. But I'm not sure now whether we talked about it or not. I don't know whether it's in the first statement, the one of the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told us a few moments ago that the question was asked. Why are you telling us now that it wasn't?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I'm -- what I'm saying now is that at this moment, I can't remember whether it was asked or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But five minutes ago, you could remember that you were asked about statements by Mr. Brdjanin. Now you've forgotten. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that now, at this moment, I cannot remember, but I know about this fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember at this point whether you were -- whether you told the investigator that you had heard Mr. Brdjanin say, "If you're not with us, you're against us"? Because that's not in your statement either, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I talked to the investigators, I couldn't remember everything. Time had elapsed. There were many events, a lot of things had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, a great deal more has happened and a lot more time has elapsed since you gave these statements, between the time you gave these statements and coming here. All of a sudden, here, you can remember all these things that you claim Mr. Brdjanin said that you couldn't remember in four days of conversations with the OTP investigator; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I told the investigators some of these statements, which I remembered at the time, but I tried to avoid thinking about what happened in Banja Luka, and then the memories surface on their own and I remember what people said. So it just comes into my head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when Ms. Richterova was questioning you on the 19th of February, page 1941, line 6 of the transcript, you were asked a question, not what you remembered about Mr. Brdjanin saying but the question is referring to Mr. Brdjanin: "Did he ever said how many of Serbs should leave Banja Luka? Said of non-Serbs should leave Banja Luka?" Now, you must have told Ms. Richterova before coming to this courtroom that you had heard that statement. When did you tell her that you had heard that statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, now I can't concentrate. I know I heard the gentleman say that in 1992. He wasn't talking about how many of them should leave Banja Luka but how many should stay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is, when did you tell Ms. Richterova that you had heard such a statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe here in the courtroom. I really don't know. But I stand by what I said. But now I'm on the edge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you want a short break to just sort of think for a moment?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for thinking, I would need ten days to calm down and to concentrate now, because this has been exhausting for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sure it has. But I think the Court would give you some time to compose yourself if you think you need it, and all you would have to do is ask for it. If you don't, then I must proceed with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that prior to your walking in here and taking the oath and starting to testify, that you had had conversations with Ms. Richterova about the testimony you would give. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the course of those conversations with Ms. Richterova, she must have asked, or you must have told her, that all of a sudden you remember Mr. Brdjanin making this statement about 3 to 5 per cent of balijas remaining. Did you tell her that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know now when I told her that, but when I talked to her, she gave me my previous statements to read through. They had been translated into Bosnian and I was asked whether I accepted them. I made two or three corrections and then I said at one point, "A person can't remember everything he saw and heard all at once." The memories surface spontaneously. And then I noticed that this statement about the percentage was not in the statement, the percentage of people who could stay. And even as we are talking now, some things surface in my memory which will perhaps disappear again tomorrow. And I think I did mention it about this percentage, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To Ms. Richterova? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was looking through the statements and making corrections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, would it be a fair statement that because of the passing of time and because of your confusion, that you don't know, as you sit here today, whether you heard Mr. Brdjanin make such a statement or you heard someone saying that Mr. Brdjanin had made such a statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard him say this personally. I will never forget it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it the truth that someone told you this after you had spoken to the OTP and you just added it to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it the truth that all these things that you claim that you heard Mr. Brdjanin say were things that you've heard from other people and that you didn't hear him say any of them?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I heard it myself from his own mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine there is a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there is no question for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't -- yeah, the microphone is on but yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would only -- I want to put into formally put into evidence our exhibits P464, P465, and P466. I didn't do it -- I didn't do it after I finished my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have -- we have them already. We have used them during the testimony of Mr. Smailagic. They are being admitted: 464, 465, 466. Is that all?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are being admitted. Mr. Ackerman, Madam Fauveau, we are talking about the indictment of Mr. Smailagic, of witness and others, for espionage in --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm familiar with the documents and I have no objection. I had earlier offered Exhibits 42A and 43 through 45, A and B, and Your Honour hasn't ruled whether they are admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want the record to show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to say about the admission of these documents and I would like to provide the DT1 document and have this admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is also being admitted as evidence in this case, being marked Exhibit DT1. Madam Registrar, now it's important to keep these documents distinct, DB and DT.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. So there are no -- there is not going to be any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, I only want to ask you whether you wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, Madam Richterova. I think it would be useful, just for the records purposes, so we can in our deliberations actually figure out whether what appears in page 1 recurs in page 2, page 3, page 4, or whether it's just a coincidence that everything happened on page 1 and not in the subsequent pages. I am in the habit of checking everything, inside out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It must have disappeared somewhere between the Prosecution and the Registry, but we submit a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem. You don't have to furnish any justification or explanation. The Chamber hasn't got any questions to put to the witness. Mr. Smailagic, I realise that this has not been easy for you, that the days you have spent in this Chamber must have tired you out. The Trial Chamber, however, would like to thank you for your kindness, for your patience, and also for all the information that you have furnished to this Trial Chamber. You may now withdraw, and I take it that your presence in The Hague will no longer be needed and arrangements will be made to escort you to wherever you need to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention, I had intended to call the investigator next to explain the system because I think it's important, but I've had Mr. Dzonlic waiting. I wonder would Your Honours care to take the break now rather than a little later so I can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have this problem, Ms. Korner. I had arranged to give a short lecture at 12.30, when we break, to all the persons that were outside in the gallery until a few minutes ago. They are being addressed by someone on my behalf in the meantime and I will be addressing them in -- at 12.30. So it will only be for 20 minutes. That's the -- I was dedicating my break to address them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In that case, Your Honour, I think what I will deal with, then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smailagic, you may withdraw. I thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand the problem is that the investigator may not be outside court because I originally said 10.00 until we had our discussion. I appreciate, even if it's only five minutes, perhaps Your Honour would care to rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We will wait outside until he turns up and then we will resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Would Your Honour forgive me just one moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the investigator will, I hope, be told -- we told him not to watch television when it became clear that he would be giving evidence in relation to this. Your Honour, can I raise, however, the translation issue that Mr. Ackerman has referred to? Like Mr. Ackerman told you that he suddenly had these documents returned to him with no notification, just to show that there is equality of arms in this Tribunal, I was informed this morning that the Translation Unit had returned, without notice to us, to Mr. Dubuisson in this Tribunal, the diary which, as Your Honour knows, has been the subject of considerable problems because it's an important document both to the Defence and the Prosecution, and, I understand, with a message that they could no longer translate any further pages. They had translated -- we prioritised the pages. In other words, we said, "On the face of it, this seems to be the important section." We had somebody read through it who understands the language, but clearly the Defence asked, and rightly, that they wanted the whole diary translated. And that, as I understand it, was agreed. Your Honour, I am now making a complaint - and I know Mr. Ackerman wants to raise something else - because firstly, it is not right for it to be returned without notification or discussion; secondly, this is so important. I appreciate that the Milosevic trial is an important one, but it cannot be right that translations, just as important for the cases of other defendants, are being, as it were, put on back burner. And I'm asking Your Honours, in fact, to make an order at this stage. Your Honours have power to make such orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we will make it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That this diary must be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are all kinds of interesting things here. One of the people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Never a dull moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the people from the Milosevic case told us yesterday that they were told that many translations they are waiting for cannot be done because there are many other cases that are going on that are taking up their time. So perhaps they are just sitting there, doing nothing. I'm not sure. I know they are not doing nothing. I know they are extraordinarily busy. There is an order in this case, entered by Judge Hunt as Pre-Trial Judge, regarding this diary, and that order is that the 1992 portions of that diary that are relevant to this case be translated in full and provided to the Defence and that the witness may not be called by the Prosecution until that is completed and until the Defence has had a full opportunity to completely review the diary. That's the order of Judge Hunt, and I don't have it in front of me so I can't give you the complete language. But my recollection is that's exactly what it says. There is an additional problem - I hesitate to raise it at this point, but I think I have some confirmation of it at least - and that is that the translation department has now said that they will translate no more books or newspaper articles. Now, if that's the case, then I would think the Prosecution should not be permitted to use any newspaper articles as evidence in this case because CLSS translated their newspaper articles and are now refusing, apparently, to translate ours, which would be an egregious denial of equality of arms that the Prosecution would get to use their newspapers articles and we couldn't. Some solution has to be found to these problems. We can't go on with a trial with these kind of things going on. I know it would be convenient to try to ignore these things, but we just can't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ackerman, I can assure you that this Trial Chamber will not ignore these things. What this Trial Chamber would require of you is to be very specific. There is only one way in which we could present the importance of this matter. Please tell us, let us know, which documents, being newspaper cuttings, you have asked to be translated and you had your request turned down. We will present it as a measure that is being taken that would deprive you of being treated equally. In other words, it would be in violation of the equality-of-arms principle, and we will give an order to that effect because we will not allow a situation to obtain in which the Prosecution is treated one way -- I'm not saying that you have even tried to be treated differently. I mean, don't misunderstand me, but we will not allow a situation to obtain whereby there is this discrepancy in treatment or difference in treatment between now and before and between you and the Prosecution or vice-versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is not something being done by the Prosecution, Your Honour, and I fully understand that. The other thing I need to inform you for the record and other purposes is that after Mr. Von Hebel suggested that we needed to do an index of these documents and send them back to CLSS, the ones that I wanted translated, I have -- we are in the process of doing a review of the newspaper articles, because they are extensive, and trying to eliminate as many as we can, and we are in fact succeeding in eliminating some of the articles. So the onus won't be quite as high as it was when I originally sent them there. So when I finally get that done and get the index completely prepared, then we will know exactly what we are sending to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in regard to that bundle of documents, Mr. Ackerman, let me be clear. As you may have noticed, we did not raise the matter again, although you know we know that at some point or another it was going to be raised and it was going to be dealt with and determined. The question is, we have postponed raising this matter further pending the arrival of this index that you are supposed to make. It's important because, in all fairness, before we can reach a decision or before we can even form an opinion, we have to accept that the CLSS department be furnished with this index, because it's on the basis of this index that we can evaluate then whether their objection to have these documents translated was at face value, at least prima facie, founded or not. After that, there are ways and means of dealing with the matter. There is the informal translations that you discussed with the Senior Legal Officer, and there are other means. However, there is also the principle of equality of arms, and particularly I think we ought to direct our attention more on this diary business than on anything else for the time being. So what I am doing now, Mrs. Jarvis, I would suggest that in the break you find for me, for us, the decision or the order made by Judge Hunt to which Mr. Ackerman has referred and we will follow up precisely from that order. You will have all the support you require, Ms. Korner, from this Trial Chamber in your regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'm told the investigator is now here, so we can carry on. Your Honour, may I ask that Mr. Dupas come into the courtroom? If Your Honours have before you the statements that Mr. Smailagic made, you will see in those his name appears on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Richard Dupas?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is also Yves Roy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to explain to Your Honours what happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the 19th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dupas, you are going to be kindly asked to make a solemn declaration that you will tell us the truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. I would imagine you are familiar with some faces in here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Richard Dupas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you work in the Office of the Prosecutor as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long have you been working here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: I've been working here for approximately 2 and a half years, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, were you a police officer in Canada?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long have you been a police officer in Canada?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: I've been a police officer for approximately 13 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dupas, I want to ask you some questions, please, about the method by which statements are taken from potential witnesses, and then direct your attention to two statements that you dealt with. Can you explain to Their Honours, first of all, the method by which a statement is actually written down, that is, taken from a witness?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, after briefing the witness as to what our intentions are for that particular interview, once we get into the actual interview process, if I am the investigator, I will direct a question to the interpreter in English, and then the interpreter will redirect the question to the witness in B/C/S. Once the witness answers in B/C/S, the interpreter will then relay his or her answer in English. And I will write that answer down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once the process is finished of question and answer, is the statement read back to the witness?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Upon completion of the interview, the statement is read back to the witness in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it the case that the statement is read back to the witness immediately at the end of the question-and-answer session or, on occasions, does something else happen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: As a general rule of thumb, Your Honours, we try to complete the interview upon meeting the witness for the first time but it does happen on occasion that the statement will not be read back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give Their Honours some examples of reasons why a statement may not be read back on the same occasion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: There are several reasons, the first one being that there simply isn't enough time to complete the full interview. Therefore, the statement will not be read back. On other occasions, such as in the course of an ongoing investigation where we will be seeing subsequent witnesses on the same mission or later on, the statement will not be read back until the full matter is properly investigated. It may also happen that the witness, upon completion of an interview, may decide suddenly that he or she does not want to sign the statement. I think those are the primary reasons why a witness would not -- or why the statement will not be signed during the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there occasions when witnesses produce documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: There are occasions, Your Honours, when witnesses will present documents, such as a diary that he or she may have written, in which case the statement will not be read back, simply because we don't have an available translation of that document. Therefore, we must return to the office and have that document properly translated before completing the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the witness is asked to sign the statement, that is after it has been read back to him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes. In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement he is asked to sign, is that the statement that you have taken in English or a translation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: I will write the statement in English, but the statement will be read back to the witness in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel for the Prosecution please make a slight pause after the answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. That's now thrown me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement itself which the witness is signing, is therefore in English?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes. It is in English. However, there is a witness acknowledgement in B/C/S that the witness will be asked to sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, other than the procedure under Rule 92 bis, where a witness is asked to attest to the truth of the contents of the statement, when is the first time normally that a witness will see a B/C/S version of the English statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Before we actually complete the Rule 92 bis declaration, before it's sworn in, the witness will be asked to read his or her statement in B/C/S prior to completing the Rule 92 bis procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for a witness who is going to be giving evidence live in this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. courtroom, when is the first time normally that they will see a version of the statement in a language that they can understand?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, the witness will be given a copy of his or her statement upon arrival here in The Hague, and normally during a proofing session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The translation of the English statement is made by whom, the interpreter who did the interpreting or by a member of the Translation Unit in this building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: The translations are always prepared by certified translators here at The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we just summarise that, Mr. Dupas, and as we are going to see with Mr. Smailagic, you can have one interpreter working on the occasion when the investigator is taking down the statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, for whatever reason, the statement is not signed on the day that it is taken and has to be read back at a later stage, that can be done by a different interpreter and indeed sometimes with a different investigator?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then there is a third interpreter involved in the sense of the translation of the statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we deal, then, please, with Mr. Smailagic's statement? I don't know whether you've brought them with you, Mr. Dupas. If not, we will give them to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dupas, we can see that your name appears on the first statement dated the 15th of April, 2000, when you had as the interpreter a lady whose name we can see there. Was that statement taken down and signed -- read back and signed on the same day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we then take the second statement, again, you were the investigator dealing with the witness. He was seen on the 4th of June, the 14th and the 19th. Now, did you see him on the first and the second occasions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first occasion, was a -- was what he said written down by you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the statement signed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very briefly, can you just tell Their Honours what the reason was why it was not signed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, Your Honours, in this particular case, I met the witness on the 4th of June and I wanted to continue with the investigation, and that is the reason why the statement was not read back to the witness on the 4th of June. I continued with my investigation between the 4th and the 14th of June, 2001, and I went back to see the witness on the 14th, to ask him some additional questions. In this particular case, the statement was not signed, simply because I did not have the time to have the statement signed. Therefore, I took some handwritten notes on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then return to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did return to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 19th of August, did a different investigator, whose name we can see, a Mr. Yves Roy, return with a different interpreter, whose name we can see, and was the read-over then done by that investigator with that interpreter and the statement was then signed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can just very briefly tell the Court where were you on the 19th of August?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: I was on holidays at that time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this investigator simply asked to deal with the reading over and the signing of the statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Dupas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many questions do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you will put them after the break, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll resume at roughly 1.00, just before 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies. Let the accused come in first. My apologies to everyone for this delay. Anyway, my apologies. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Maglov is back in the courtroom and I took the liberty of asking her to come back but I need to get your permission for her to remain here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have personally, for the moment, nothing to add to what we added last time. I have to inform you that matter has been referred to the office that deals with the -- to the Registry, anyway, to the Registrar, and as soon as we get some kind of feedback from there, we will take the matter up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was important was that during the evidence of Mr. Smailagic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. And the rest will -- we will talk about later if we need to. So can you call the witness in, please? Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman? Mr. Ackerman, by the way, Mr. Dupas, is counsel for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dupas.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How are you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: I'm fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have just very few, I think, questions to ask you. The process that you have described the way these statements are taken, you ask a question, the witness through a translator answers, and then you write down the answer. I assume you write it down in longhand or do you put it on a computer or how do you do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: It depends. In certain circumstances, Your Honours, I would take handwritten notes. In other circumstances, I can type live. That is to say, when the interpreter gives me an answer in English, I will type the answer directly on the computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you do this -- do you just make a note or do you write down word for word what the witness says?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: It's always word for word. That is to say word for word, the answer that the interpreter relays from the answer of the witness, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you suggesting to the Chamber that there are frequent errors with regard to interpretation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that, Your Honours. I don't know if it's a mistake with the interpretation or not, as I don't understand the language of the witness. All I can say is that the answer that the interpreter will give me after a witness answers a question, I will type the answer given to me by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we start with a question in English that is translated into B/C/S, that is then answered in B/C/S and translated back into English and then typed on to a paper, and then given to someone who has no association with that process at all, to translate it back into B/C/S? That's the way it works, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I've understood everything you've asked but I will say -- I can repeat the process once again, that is when I ask a question, the interpreter will relay my question. I always ask my question in English and the interpreter will always relay my question in B/C/S. The witness will answer in B/C/S. And then the interpreter will relay his answer in English to me and I will type the answer given to me by the interpreter on to either a piece of paper or I will type it on a computer. I'm not sure that that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's close enough. Has anybody ever suggested that it might be a good idea to record what the witness says in B/C/S so that we can have an accurate record of what the witness says?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: I'm not really sure I know what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say "record," I mean electronically record what the witness says in B/C/S so the witness won't then be able to come here and claim that they didn't say it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Right. Your Honours, I did understand that part. What I didn't understand, if -- has someone ever suggested to me that this was the way to do it. I'm not really sure what you're asking there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Has someone ever suggested that that's the way to do it, to you or to anyone else, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Suggested, no. This is the process that I've just described to Your Honours is the process that is adopted by the Office of the Prosecutor, and that is the process that we use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not record what the witness says in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: In this particular statement, I record in English. I record it in English the answers given to me by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the recording won't have the witness's answer in B/C/S on it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: The statement will reflect the answers given to me by the interpreter and I presume that this is the answer given to the interpreter by the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now I'm confused. Do you have an electronic device that records what the witness says when you're taking these statements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. In this particular case, if we are talking about Mr. Smailagic's statement, I did not have an electronic recording device. The only electronic device that I had was my computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that with regard to some statements, you in fact do record what the witness says in his own language or her own language?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: There are processes. There are instances, when we interview a witness, where that interview will be recorded, that is audio recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It must be that it is not a secret in the Office of the Prosecutor that this process of multiple translations is less than satisfactory. It just -- I just don't understand why it hasn't -- there hasn't been a process to record the statements in the original language from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that's really for this investigator to answer. It's a matter of policy which if Mr. Ackerman wants to take it up with those in charge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to stop him, Ms. Korner, and I will now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, then, when I look at a statement, and it says, "I was receiving threatening phone calls at my home almost on a daily basis," that those, to the best of your ability, are the exact words at least that you heard from the translator who was translating the witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: That would be the answer, or that is to say, the response to a particular question. In this case, would have been the answer given to me, relayed to me by the interpreter, and I would have typed it down word for word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you get to the point where the statement has been typed, and you are showing it to the witness to get him to sign it, what do you do when the witness says, "Well, here on page 7, that paragraph is incorrect"? Do you then completely redo do the statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't completely redo the statement, Your Honours. I would ask the interpreter, or I would ask the question, pose the question to the witness, what exactly isn't correct in the paragraph or the line that the witness wants to correct. And I would clarify that part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm looking at a piece of paper that has a statement on it. I assume this is the piece of paper that is translated to the witness and the witness is asked to sign. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if the witness says on page 7, paragraph 3, "That is not what I said, that's not correct," what do you do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: When you meet a witness for the first time, or in this particular case, when I met a witness, if I was to meet a witness and we're actually doing the read back that particular day, that is to say completing the full interview, and a witness during the read back would point out something that isn't correct or that the witness would like to change in his statement, then you would make the correction before reading back the statement, before the witness actually signs it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't notice in any of these statements that something is crossed out and something added. Do you completely retype the statement at that point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: No. As I previously mentioned, Your Honours, during the read back, if the witness is unsatisfied with something, with an answer that is read back to him, I would make the correction right there and then and retype the part of the statement that the witness would like to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I'm confused, Mr. Dupas. If you'll look at the statement that we are looking at, for instance, the first statement of this witness Mr. Smailagic, it goes from page 1 through 7, and then there is -- actually, there is 1 through 8 because there is acknowledgements at the end?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may help because of the time, I know that we have been strictly enjoined to finish by quarter to 2, if I -- I'm giving evidence but I would ask the investigator to confirm it. The read back - that may be the confusion - is done from a computer screen, not a piece of paper. There is no printed out. In other words, when the interpreter reads back to a witness the statement, it's the computer screen they are reading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's the case, you're reading -- they are reading from a computer screen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when is the witness actually handed a hard copy and asked to sign it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Once the read back has been completed, and the witness agrees that all of the information in the statement that was taken there and then is correct, then the investigator should give a copy, that is to say a hard copy, of the statement and the witness is asked to sign the statement once everything is agreed upon, that is to say the facts in the statement are correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have a printer with you, you can print it out right there on the scene?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you took one statement from Mr. Smailagic on 15 April, 2000 and then went back in June of 2001 to talk to him some more. And he has indicated that at that time you suggested to him that some of the things he'd said in his first statement were apparently untrue. For instance, the -- his assertion that Brdjanin's wife was named Perka. And what you do, I guess, after you take a statement from a witness is make some effort at least to check out some of the things that have been said, and then take the opportunity to inform the witness that there are some things the witness said that may not be correct and give the witness a chance to correct those things. Is that a fair statement? That's a pretty long statement. I'm sure you heard it all.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Your Honours, I think Mr. Ackerman wants me to -- the question that you're -- that Mr. Ackerman is asking me, is if I go back once -- I go back to The Hague and I verify some of the facts that the witness has given me and/or told to me, and once I verified those and I find out or I discover that some of the facts that the witness has relayed to me are inaccurate or not complete, then I would go back and meet the witness and clarify. If that's what Mr. Ackerman is asking me, then that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is what he --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's exactly what I asked, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: That would be a fair statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When you actually do record, electronically record, the statements of a witness in their native language, I take it you preserve those recordings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: Well, the preservation of the -- Your Honours, the preservation of the witness statement is not in his or her -- in the witness's language. It's always in the English language. And there is an electronic version of the statement that is kept in our team files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, what I'm referring to is when you not record on computer but record the actual voice of the witness. When you make actual voice recordings or video recordings of a statement of a witness, I assume those voice recordings or video recordings are preserved. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD DUPAS
utterances.text: When there is an audio recorded interview of a witness, Your Honours, taken, there is a copy that is preserved, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maitre Pitron or Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any additional questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Maitre Pitron. I think if there are no further questions, the witness may withdraw. I thank you, Mr. Dupas. You have been most helpful. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was going to suggest, I hope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was hoping to give the order with regard to the diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In that case, Your Honour, there is clearly no opportunity to call the next witness, so he can be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the diary issue is more important. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start from here because this will be an oral order that we will have to make. You informed the Trial Chamber this morning that you had received a diary from -- would you again repeat the information that you gave to the Trial Chamber this morning with regard to this diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this morning our office, the person responsible for translations, received two packages -- I'm sorry, three, I'm corrected by Ms. Richterova, three packages containing the remaining part of the diary. As I understand the matter, it was accompanied by a note from Mr. Dubuisson -- no, in that case I think Ms. Richterova dealt with it, if she explains it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah, we received, it wasn't this morning, it was yesterday, we received three packages with a memo from Christina Zoric from CLSS, addressed to Mark Dubuisson, and it was a memo stating that CLSS cannot deal with these translation, and on these three packages was yellow stickers, stating the name of the person from trial support, without any explanation why these three packages ended up in the trial support. That's all. And we were advised by Registry that there is a memo with an explanation, but we have never got such an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I spoke with Mr. Dubuisson, who is my chief and chief of court management and support services section. He explained to me the following. First, the diary was given to CLSS in three parts. One was the first priority, which was completed. The second group, they are still working on the translations. And the third part of that diary, which consists of 500 to 700 pages, was given back to the Prosecution, explaining that they were unable to complete the translation at that moment. And I'm waiting for the memo to be produced. He also informed me that they have a working group dealing with these issues on translation and document control, in order to prioritise documents and in order that they are translated. So this is the official response from the Registry. Now, I explained to him that in fact you may want to issue an oral order based on the information, and that he said there is no problem with giving back the third batch of documents or, excuse me, the third part of the diary to be translated. I guess the issue then becomes when you will get it back from translation. I think that's the critical issue at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go slowly because [Microphone not activated]. This has to be oral [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go slowly. I will be trying to summarise first the information that is -- has been given by the Prosecution. In the course of this morning's session, the Prosecution informed this Trial Chamber that it had received three bundles of documents forming part of the diary that the CLSS has been translating, a diary to which previous proceedings in the Pre-Trial stage refer, with an intimation that the CLSS was not in a position to continue translating the remaining pages of the said diary. For the time being, does that more or less reflect correctly, more or less, what you have reported to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. This Trial Chamber has also been informed that there is a memo purporting to explain the reason behind the decision of the CLSS to return the said documents to the Prosecution, although no one has been in a position to show this memo to the Trial Chamber this morning. The Trial Chamber wishes to refer to the decision of -- to its decision of the 15th November, 2001, in which inter alia, in paragraph 5 of the same it was decided that, "It is certainly only fair that counsel for Brdjanin should have the entire diary translated into English in sufficient time before he has to cross-examine Witness 7.207." "...the issue as to whether it should be permitted to call Witness 7.207 at all in the circumstances which have been related can only be determined at the stage it is known when the entire diary will be or has been translated into English and an assessment can be made as to how long Brdjanin's counsel will reasonably need to read it for the purpose of cross-examining the witness." The Trial Chamber further notes that it was possible to start this trial on schedule and it was previously possible to fix a schedule for the commencement of this trial precisely because there was forthcoming an assurance to this Trial Chamber of a steady flow of translations of this diary forthcoming from the CLSS on a regular basis and as indicated by CLSS and the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber is of the opinion that any interruption in the flow of the process of translation of this diary at this stage or at any further stage of these proceedings would, given the present circumstances, seriously compromise the progress of this trial and has the potentiality, if not the certainty, of bringing this trial to an undesirable halt. The Trial Chamber further feels, or is of the opinion, that the decision of the CLSS to return the diary, or the remaining parts, the untranslated remaining parts of the diary to the Prosecution with the said intimation that they would not be proceeding with the translation of same at any identified time runs counter to the above-mentioned decision of this Trial Chamber of the 15th of November, 2001, and in effect would nullify the whole purpose for which the same decision was handed down. The Trial Chamber therefore requests the Prosecution to return the said documents to the CLSS and is giving instructions to the same department, CLSS, to proceed with -- to proceed with the translation of the remaining part of the diary that has not yet been translated, and to conclude the exercise in good time without prejudicing the progress or continuation of this trial. For the purpose of this order, it is suggested to the CLSS to coordinate with the Prosecution and with the Defence, which should be in a position to give an indication as to how early the complete translation is required for the purposes of this trial. I think we could leave it at that. I can't give you anything better than this because I would have to sit down and write a judgement, an order, and I don't think we should waste more time on it. It deserves priority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will continue tomorrow, we will resume tomorrow -- sorry, not tomorrow, on Monday. We will resume on Monday with the evidence, testimony of Mr. Dzonlic. And I would suggest that you more or less agree on the documents that would be made use of, at least by the Prosecution, for the purpose of the examination in chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's been done and Your Honour has been given a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have, yes. I don't know whether the Defence has. Okay, I thank you once more and we will have a nice weekend, long weekend, and we will all meet on Monday morning. Including Maitre Pitron?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as Mr. de Roux said to you, I think, the Defence, the French Defence team shall maintain in permanence or quasi-permanence the presence of Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic. That will be guaranteed. And Mr. De Roux and myself shall come here regularly to continue with our efforts and to try to persuade you. It's probably that on Monday and Tuesday, I will be absent. On Monday, I will be absent but we will be here during the second part of the week, and what I suggest out of courtesy is that we should inform you, in advance, which members of the Defence team, of the French Defence team, will be present at your hearings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be appreciated, Maitre Pitron, and it would also be appreciated if you keep your client informed precisely on what the plans are, because it is important and he has a right to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will meet on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
